He looked down. “...When the fuck did this place have a wading pool?” The water lapped above the arch of his foot. It had soaked through his socks. Not just wet...murky. Almost oily. It caught what little light the buzzing overhead fixture offered, dark and absolutely still. How had he not noticed that? It wasn’t very deep, but it was more than enough that he should have noticed while he was elbow deep in generator grease. So how the fuck did he MISS that? He took another look around the room, lightly clenching one fist in idle twitchiness from the mix of mold smell and the persistent heavy heartbeat thrum from the killer upstairs. That was enough. There were other generators in other buildings and none of them were currently trying to give him a feeling he couldn't shake. They could leave this one to whoever else had pulled Bedham tonight and go find something less — whatever this was. “Right. Nope. I’m out.” He backed away from the generator with abrupt finality. “Too wet. Too quiet. Too weird. I’m not getting trench foot for a basement gen. Back upstairs. We can go do one of the 2nd story house gens. You with me?” Dwight blinked, pulled his attention back. “Yeah. Sorry.” He shook out his hands as if they’d gone numb. “We can do a different house. It’s—” He made a face. “—gross down here.” “Gross I can do,” David said. “This is... extra.” He flicked a glance toward the stairs they’d come down. “Let’s try upstairs before it turns into any more of a sauna.” He took a breath to ask if David felt it too, if the room was wrong, if he’d imagined the hallway getting longer; but David was already headed for the stairs. Dwight put a palm on the wall as he reached the bottom step, and the concrete felt warmer than it should have. Body-warm. He wiped his hand on his jeans and pretended the fabric hadn’t already stuck to his knee. David made it partway up before slipping back into a crouch and pressing against the wall before the stairs bent to go up. Danny was sitting at the top, just above the landing. Phone in hand. Legs swinging lazily. Silently thumbing through an app like he was waiting for a bus. Not stealthed, not hunting — just there, in the worst possible place, with all the awareness of someone who had never seriously considered that anything might be coming up those stairs toward him. David waved Dwight back, patting his chest quick and pointing up. Terror heartbeat straight ahead. Of course, the killer would be right there. It would be their luck that Danny had gotten bored with trashing the place and had settled in to play games on his phone for half a trial. The boys shared a look, weighing options. The basement, with its wrong angles and weird light and inch of standing water, waited behind them. These stairs were clearly a no-go. That left the pipe hallway hole and the far back steps. The hole in the hallway ceiling wasn’t reachable from the ground, and even if they could scramble up to it, the hall it was in was directly down from the stairs. Trying to pass by Ghostface with a clear line of sight was a gamble at the best of times. Dude was entirely too quick and wily. “Other stairs,” David mouthed silently, jerking his chin towards the pipe hallway. Dwight nodded briskly and followed David into the mini-maze, only relaxing slightly when the terror radius calmed from a panicked hammering into a background thump, before fading away entirely. The air in the hallway was worse; stale and wet and sharp, the kind of smell that curled behind your eyes. Pipes creaked above them, old and half-rotted. Twice, they had to duck surprise sprays of water as valves burst open in sharp, echoing snaps. The steam made the walls sweat. Dwight had almost immediately lost all sense of the room's geometry. The hallway had always been easy to get turned around in — he knew that, had been in it before — but something about the proportions felt wrong in a way that went beyond the usual tangle of valves and junctions. The walls were the right color, the pipes were the right rust, and somehow none of it added up to a space that felt like it should exist. Valves hissed as they passed. One of them let out a sudden spray that soaked David’s shoulder, making him flinch and swear again. “Didn’t this used to be a lot shorter?” “Layout changes,” Dwight murmured, slightly relieved that it wasn’t just him that had noticed. “It happens. The domains shift sometimes. Usually between trials, but..." He trailed off, looking at the way the hallway kept going into the dark past the edge of what the light could reach. "Usually between trials." “Yeah, well, I don’t like this version.” There was no echo to their footfalls anymore. Just wet slaps swallowed by the space. David kept glancing at the pipes, brow furrowed in clear distrust, murmuring half to himself. The second room was somehow worse than the first. The water had found their ankles somewhere in the pipe hallway and followed them through, and by the time they cleared the last junction it was sitting just above — cool against the humid press of the air, which was somehow both damp and warm in a way that made no sense for a basement. The overhead light buzzed its flat, dying note. Dwight looked up, but the bulb wasn’t flickering. It was just making that sound anyway, as it cast oddly angled shadows over the lockers that lined the wall. The stairs were gone. Not literally, but effectively.
